newsitem.title: JAPAN: Gap between Japan's regional banks widening - S&P.
newsitem.headline: Gap between Japan's regional banks widening - S&P.

text.p: The gap between the asset quality of Japan's big regional banks and their smaller rivals has widened, and the plight of the smaller banks could hurt the nation's banking industry, Standard & Poor's said on Tuesday.
There are 64 first-tier regional banks and 65 second-tier regional banks in Japan.
The bigger regional banks generally have a relatively healthy financial profile, S&P said in a report.

However, concerning second-tier regional banks, it said that those with relatively sound asset quality would probably survive in their current form through restructuring, but "it will be tough for banks plagued with serious asset quality problems and vulnerable funding positions to continue operating".

Concerning the impact of such a situation on the nation's banking industry, S&P said recent instances of the bailouts of several second-tier regional banks such as Hyogo Bank and Taiheiyo Bank have forced big nationwide banks to shoulder the financial burdens of the second-tier banks.
"If similar bailouts become necessary, the impact on larger institutions could be formidable," S&P said.

Noting the Ministry of Finance's (MOF) estimate that second-tier banks' problem loans totalled 2.41 trillion yen, or 4.58 percent of the total loans they had extended as of end-March 1996, S&P said the ratio would be higher than MOF's figure under S&P's definition.
S&P said tier-one regional banks are sustained by broad-based lending and sound asset quality as well as satisfactory capitalisation and core profitability.

Quoting MOF estimates, it said the proportion of problem loans, including restructured loans, at the tier-one banks was 3.1 percent, lower than the banking industry average of 4.9 percent, as of the end of March.
